prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map shows a narrow corner space with a concrete floor about 1.5–1.8 metres below the camera wearer, bordered by open closet shelves and white drawers on the left (0.5–1.2 metres away), a swinging white door in front/above (0.3–1.0 metres away), and a brick wall and doorway threshold on the right (1.0–1.8 metres away). The camera wearer's own torso and gloved arms appear brightest in the lower foreground at 0.2–0.7 metres, while a second person stands to the bottom-right at roughly 1.0–1.5 metres from the wearer and 0.5–0.8 metres from the right-hand doorway, with their head and upper body cropped out of the right frame edge. Across the five frames, the wearer's left hand pushes the white door in Frame 1 and Frame 2 (within arm's reach at ~0.5–0.7 metres) causing the door to swing away toward the right from Frame 1 to Frame 4 before bouncing slightly back in Frame 5, while the wearer's left hand moves down in Frame 3 to join the right hand on a long-handled broom/scraper reaching the floor (~0.4–1.5 metres away). Meanwhile, the second person on the right shifts slightly away from the wearer in Frame 4 before stepping right and partially behind the door in Frame 5, facing generally toward the corner/left and never looking up at the high head-mounted camera. Compared to RGB, the depth map clearly separates the foreground silhouette of the wearer, the swinging door plane, and the recessed floor corner, though it is unreliable on thin structures like the broom handle's lower half and blurs the shelves and small floor objects (like the drill near the door hinge and paper towels on the left shelf) into smooth gradients.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates only foreground human regions (`person`) against a black background, capturing the camera wearer's downward-viewed torso, shoulders, and gloved arms at 0.2–0.7 metres in the lower-left/center of all five frames. In Frames 1 and 2, the pink mask tracks the wearer's extended left arm reaching forward and up to the door edge (~0.6 metres away) and their right hand holding the broom handle on the right, then shows both arms converging in front of the torso at 0.3–0.5 metres in Frames 3–5 as the left hand moves onto the lower handle. All surrounding scene structures—including the closet shelves with paper towels within arm's reach on the left (~0.5–0.8 metres), the swinging white door in front, the floor below (~1.6 metres), and the broom handle itself—are omitted as unlabelled background. The map is highly unreliable for the second person standing ~1.0–1.5 metres to the lower-right (whose torso and legs are partly occluded by the right frame edge and face roughly toward the wearer/corner), completely failing to detect them in Frames 1–3 and Frame 5. Only in Frame 4 does a second brown `person` mask appear, where it inaccurately merges the wearer's right arm with fragments of the second person's legs and torso across a ~0.8-metre gap while still providing cleaner foreground human-boundary separation in the first three frames than raw RGB clutter.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is almost entirely blank across all five frames, detecting only a single compact cluster of yellow keypoints in the lower-left of Frame 1 at roughly 1.0–1.4 metres below the camera and 0.8 metres to the left of the second person. In the RGB context—where the camera wearer looks steeply downward past their own torso and gloved hands (0.2–0.7 metres away) toward the floor (~1.6 metres below) and a second person stands cropped at the lower-right (~1.0–1.5 metres away)—neither person's head or face is oriented toward the camera, and severe self-occlusion and steep top-down foreshortening hide normal full-body proportions. Across Frames 1 to 5, as the wearer's left hand leaves the door (Frames 1–2) to grip the broom shaft with both hands (Frames 3–5) and the second person shifts near the right doorway threshold, the pose estimator fails to track either the wearer's arms, the magenta hand skeletons, or the second person's lower body in Frames 2–5. The solitary yellow skeleton in Frame 1 is an unreliable, hallucinated miniature body pose triggered by the camera wearer's left shoe and floor edges (or nearby shelf clutter), offering no usable spatial information beyond indicating a false-positive detection near the wearer's left foot.
